title: Load Balancing, Firewalls, and Intrusion Protection
bodyMarkdown:
## Distribute first, then defend in layers

Once the network exists, you put a load balancer in front of the workload and layer controls around it: a WAF at the edge, policy-based firewalls inside the VPC, NAT for egress, and detection for what slips through. Exam questions in this area rarely ask for a definition; they hand you a requirement ("single anycast IP", "preserve client IP", "folder-wide guardrails", "detect lateral movement") and expect you to pick the one product whose properties match.

## Choosing a load balancer

Google Cloud load balancers vary along four axes: **protocol layer** (Application is L7 HTTP/HTTPS; Network is L4), **proxy versus passthrough**, **scope** (global, cross-region, regional) and **exposure** (external or internal). The [load balancer selection guide](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/choosing-load-balancer) organizes the portfolio into three families.

| Family | Layer and protocols | Deployments | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Application Load Balancer | L7: HTTP and HTTPS | Global external; regional external; regional internal; cross-region internal | Proxy-based; URL maps; Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor on external types |
| Proxy Network Load Balancer | L4: TCP, with optional SSL offload | Global external; regional external; regional internal; cross-region internal | Proxy-based; terminates the client connection |
| Passthrough Network Load Balancer | L4: TCP, UDP, ESP, GRE, ICMP (internal also SCTP and AH) | Regional external; internal | Does not terminate connections; preserves client source IP |

A few details that matter in questions:

- A **global external** Application or Proxy Network LB uses the **Premium Network Service Tier** and gives you one anycast address that fronts backends in many regions. Regional external deployments can run on Premium or Standard tier. Standard tier is regional only and cheaper for workloads without strict latency needs.
- **Scope drives resilience.** Global and cross-region load balancers survive a regional outage; a regional load balancer survives only zonal failures.
- The **global external passthrough** Network LB is listed as Preview in the selection guide at time of writing, so do not design a production answer around it.
- Application LBs terminate TLS (including Google-managed certificates), route by host, path, headers and other request parameters through **URL maps**, and support backends such as managed instance groups, zonal, serverless, hybrid and internet NEGs, Cloud Storage buckets, and Cloud Run. The [Application Load Balancer documentation](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/application-load-balancer) also lists Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor and frontend mutual TLS.

**Decision rules:**

1. Internet HTTP(S), worldwide, one IP, CDN, WAF: **global external Application LB**.
2. Microservice HTTP(S) inside the VPC: **regional internal Application LB** (or cross-region internal for multi-region failover).
3. Non-HTTP TCP needing proxy features such as SSL offload: **Proxy Network LB**.
4. TCP or UDP where the backend must see the real client IP, or protocols like ESP and GRE: **passthrough Network LB**.
5. Proxy load balancers do not preserve client IPs by default; if the question is "preserve the client source IP", passthrough is the signal.

## Firewall layers

Google Cloud evaluates several kinds of firewall rules. Knowing their scope and order resolves most questions.

| Mechanism | Attaches to | Targets | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hierarchical firewall policy | Organization or folder | Resources in descendant projects | Org-wide guardrails that project owners cannot override |
| Global or regional network firewall policy | A VPC network (global) or region of it | VMs by tags, service accounts, or secure tags | Reusable rule sets per network |
| [VPC firewall rules](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls) | One VPC network | All instances, network tags, or service accounts | Classic per-network rules |

Facts to know cold:

- VPC firewall rules are **stateful**: if a connection is allowed in either direction, matching return traffic is allowed. Rule priority runs **0 to 65,535**, default **1000**, lower number wins.
- Network tags are editable by anyone who can edit the instance; a **service account** target is a stronger identity because only one service account can be attached to an instance. A single VPC firewall rule cannot mix tag targets and service account targets.
- Default evaluation order (`AFTER_CLASSIC_FIREWALL`): hierarchical policies (organization, then folders), regional system policies, **VPC firewall rules**, global network firewall policies, regional network firewall policies, then implied actions. An alternative `BEFORE_CLASSIC_FIREWALL` enforcement order moves network policies ahead of VPC rules. See the [firewall policy evaluation order](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-rule-eval-order).
- Within a layer rules are processed from highest to lowest priority and evaluation stops at the first allow, deny, or `apply_security_profile_group`. The `goto_next` action hands the decision to the next layer, and no match behaves as an implicit `goto_next`. This is how a security team writes "deny unless a lower layer opts in".
- Implied actions at the end: egress **allowed**, ingress to a VM **denied**, ingress to a load balancer forwarding rule **allowed**.
- The [firewall policies overview](https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewall-policies-overview) describes Cloud Next Generation Firewall (NGFW), which adds Layer 7 inspection through security profile groups.

## Edge protection and detection

- **[Cloud Armor](https://cloud.google.com/armor/docs/cloud-armor-overview)** applies security policies at the Google edge, close to the traffic source, in front of external Application LBs (all types), regional internal Application LBs, global external proxy Network LBs, and regional external passthrough Network LBs. Capabilities include preconfigured WAF rules (OWASP-based signatures), rate limiting, IP and geo allow or deny, and bot management. It gives always-on protection from L3 and L4 volumetric DDoS; L7 protection such as HTTP flood mitigation requires configured policies. Standard and Enterprise tiers differ (Enterprise adds Adaptive Protection, threat intelligence feeds, and richer telemetry).
- **[Cloud IDS](https://cloud.google.com/intrusion-detection-system/docs/overview)** is a managed intrusion **detection** service built on Palo Alto Networks threat prevention (App-ID and signatures updated daily). It mirrors traffic with Packet Mirroring to Google-managed inspection VMs and sees both north-south and east-west traffic. An IDS endpoint is a zonal resource, handles about 5 Gbps, and Google recommends one endpoint per 5 Gbps of throughput. Alerts have five severities from Critical to Informational. Critically, it **detects and alerts but does not block**; enforcement comes from Cloud NGFW or other controls. Layer 7 inspection policies from Cloud NGFW take priority over overlapping IDS policies.
- **[Cloud NAT](https://cloud.google.com/nat/docs/overview)** gives VMs without external IPs outbound access. It is a distributed, software-defined service (no proxy VMs), is created per region on a Cloud Router, and allows only established return traffic, never unsolicited inbound connections. Public NAT reaches the internet; private NAT translates between private networks (VPCs, on-premises, other clouds).
- **[Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/concepts-overview)** is an application-level access layer: it authenticates and authorizes each request by identity and group instead of by network location, so no VPN is needed for internal web apps. Users need the **IAP-secured Web App User** role, and context-aware access can add device and location conditions. It fronts App Engine, Cloud Run, GKE and Compute Engine behind a load balancer, and is only as strong as its enforcement: firewall the backends to the load balancer and disable the `run.app` URL, or callers bypass it. For admin access, [IAP TCP forwarding](https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/using-tcp-forwarding) tunnels SSH and RDP to VMs with **no external IP** (allow ingress from `35.235.240.0/20` on ports 22 and 3389; the user needs the IAP-secured Tunnel User role), replacing bastion hosts. It is not for bulk data transfer.
- **[VPC Service Controls](https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview)** builds service perimeters around Google-managed services to reduce data exfiltration. It works independently of IAM, includes dry-run mode, ingress and egress rules, and access levels. It is **not a firewall** and does not protect third-party or internet endpoints.

## Edge delivery: Cloud CDN and Network Service Tiers

[Cloud CDN](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/overview) caches content at Google's edge for the global external Application Load Balancer (and the classic one), with backend services (instance groups, GKE) and Cloud Storage backend buckets as origins. Facts to know:

- **Cache modes:** `CACHE_ALL_STATIC` (default) caches static content that is not otherwise uncacheable; `USE_ORIGIN_HEADERS` caches only responses with valid cache directives; `FORCE_CACHE_ALL` caches successful responses and overrides the origin. See [caching](https://cloud.google.com/cdn/docs/caching).
- **Defaults:** TTL 3,600 seconds when the origin sends no header, maximum TTL 86,400 seconds, negative caching off. Invalidation removes cached objects before expiry.
- Cloud Armor works with it, and Cloud CDN is available only on the **Premium** tier.

[Network Service Tiers](https://cloud.google.com/network-tiers/docs/overview) set how traffic between the internet and your resources is routed:

| | Premium (default) | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| Routing | Google backbone; traffic enters at the point of presence nearest the user | Public internet routing; enters at the resource's region |
| Scope | Global or regional addresses | Regional only |
| Load balancers | All external types, including global | Regional external only (not global, no Cloud CDN) |
| Pick when | Latency, global reach, CDN | Cost-sensitive, single-region, not latency-critical |

Moving a resource between tiers changes its IP address, because the tiers use separate address pools.

## Putting the layers together

A hardened internet-facing application typically combines: a global external Application LB with Cloud Armor in front; backends in private subnets with no external IPs; Cloud NAT for outbound patching; hierarchical policies for non-negotiable guardrails and network policies or VPC rules for app-specific allows; Cloud IDS for detection; and a VPC Service Controls perimeter around BigQuery and Cloud Storage holding the data. Each control covers a different failure mode, so none replaces another.

## Scenario walkthroughs

**Global retail site under bot and flood traffic.** Users worldwide, one IP, URL-based routing to a catalog service and a checkout service, and a requirement to block SQL injection patterns and abusive clients. Answer: global external Application LB with a URL map, Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules (these are OWASP-oriented signatures compiled from open-source standards such as the Core Rule Set) plus rate limiting, backends in private subnets. Cloud IDS is not the answer because the requirement is to block, and it only alerts.

**Internal payment microservices.** HTTP(S) calls between services in one region, no internet exposure, path-based routing. Answer: regional internal Application LB. If the services must stay reachable after a regional failure, the cross-region internal Application LB is the variant built for that. Cloud Armor still applies to the regional internal Application LB, which is relevant if you need WAF rules on internal traffic.

**Folder of regulated projects.** The security team wants every project under a folder to block inbound SSH from the internet regardless of what project owners do, while letting teams add their own application rules. Answer: a hierarchical firewall policy on the folder with a deny rule, and VPC firewall rules or network firewall policies for team-specific allows. Use `goto_next` in the hierarchical policy for traffic you want lower layers to decide, so you do not accidentally hard-code every team's needs at the top.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Using Cloud IDS as a blocker.** It only detects and alerts. Prevention needs Cloud Armor at the edge or NGFW and firewall policies inside the VPC.
- **Putting Cloud Armor on everything.** It protects specific load balancer types; it does not sit in front of VM-to-VM traffic inside the VPC.
- **Project-level rules for org-wide mandates.** Project owners can edit those. Use hierarchical policies at the organization or folder.
- **Tag-based targeting for security boundaries.** Anyone with instance-edit rights can change tags; use service accounts (or secure tags).
- **Choosing a proxy load balancer when the backend needs client IPs.** Pick passthrough, or forward the address in headers with an Application LB.
- **Calling VPC Service Controls a firewall.** It is an API-level data perimeter for Google-managed services, complementary to IAM and firewalls.
- **Treating IAP as network security.** Leave a VM or `run.app` URL reachable directly and IAP is bypassed; restrict ingress to the load balancer.
- **Choosing Standard tier for a global audience.** It cannot host a global load balancer or Cloud CDN; pick Premium.
- **Expecting Cloud NAT to accept inbound connections.** Publishing a service needs a load balancer or PSC, not NAT.
- **Relying on the implied rules.** Ingress deny is implied for VMs but ingress to a load balancer forwarding rule is allowed; write explicit rules.

## Exam tips

- **Global HTTP(S) with one IP, CDN and URL routing:** global external Application LB. Regional passthrough is the classic distractor.
- **Preserve client source IP or non-HTTP protocols:** passthrough Network LB. Proxy types terminate the connection.
- **Hierarchy means hierarchical firewall policies.** Attached to organization or folder, evaluated before VPC rules, cannot be overridden by project owners.
- **Cloud IDS detects, Cloud Armor and firewalls prevent.** If the question demands blocking, IDS alone is wrong; if it demands deep L7 visibility east-west, IDS is right.
- **Cloud Armor is edge WAF and DDoS for load balancers.** It needs a supported LB in front; L7 attack mitigation needs configured policies.
- **Private VMs with outbound updates:** Cloud NAT. It is outbound-only, regional, on a Cloud Router, and uses no proxy VMs.
- **Prefer service accounts over tags** for firewall targets when the scenario stresses tamper resistance or least privilege.
- **Identity-based access to internal web apps or SSH without VPN or external IPs:** Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP-secured Web App User; IAP TCP forwarding for VMs). Block direct access to backends.
- **Cloud CDN and global load balancing need Premium tier;** Standard is regional and cheaper. Default cache mode is `CACHE_ALL_STATIC`.
- **VPC Service Controls is a data-exfiltration perimeter,** not a network firewall and not a replacement for IAM.
